title: Forced Navier–Stokes blow-up at a no-slip wall
W: In 2026 it was shown that a smooth, compactly supported force can drive the 3D Navier–Stokes equations, started from rest, to blow up in finite time. Inside a domain this can simply be copied away from any wall. Show that blow-up can also happen at the wall itself: in a half-space with the no-slip condition, the velocity becomes unbounded at a point of the boundary.

why: The 2026 forced blow-up of Navier–Stokes is an interior, axisymmetric-vortex construction; inside a domain it can be placed in a ball away from the boundary, so interior blow-up in bounded domains or half-spaces is already essentially available. The no-slip wall is where real flows generate vorticity (boundary layers, Prandtl theory) and where regularity theory is weakest (e.g. Seregin–Šverák boundary criteria), so a boundary singularity would test whether the mechanism survives the vanishing of velocity on the wall.
issues: Original M allowed interior blow-up, which follows from Cao–Chi–Nie (arXiv 2609.10262, Sect. 3.7: blow-up balls inside bounded domains with no-slip) by placing the OpenAI construction away from the wall; tightened to require the singular set on the boundary. Specified force class (smooth up to the wall, compact support in time positive), solution class, finite energy, and meaning of blow-up. No paper found constructing a boundary singularity; related work (Kang, Chang–Kang on singular velocity near boundary for localized forces) gives non-blow-up boundary singular behaviour for weak solutions.

title: Kagome Hofstadter butterfly
W: Electrons hopping on the square lattice in a magnetic field have a Cantor-set spectrum for every irrational flux (the Ten Martini problem, Avila–Jitomirskaya), and the same is now known for the honeycomb lattice of graphene. Prove it for the kagome lattice in a uniform magnetic field.
M: Let $\Lambda$ be the kagome lattice with nearest-neighbour bonds of length $1/2$ (sites $\mathbb Z a_1+\mathbb Z a_2+\{0,a_1/2,a_2/2\}$, $a_1=(1,0)$, $a_2=(\tfrac12,\tfrac{\sqrt3}2)$). For a constant magnetic field $B$ with vector potential $A$, set $(H_B\psi)(x)=\sum_{y\sim x}e^{i\int_{[x,y]}A}\psi(y)$ on $\ell^2(\Lambda)$, and write $2\pi\alpha=B\,|a_1\wedge a_2|$ for the flux per unit cell (so each triangle carries flux $2\pi\alpha/8$ and each hexagon $2\pi\cdot 6\alpha/8$). Prove that $\sigma(H_B)$ is a Cantor set (nonempty, compact, perfect, nowhere dense) for every irrational $\alpha$.
why: Cantor spectrum for the Harper model (Ten Martini, Avila–Jitomirskaya) and for graphene (Becker–Han–Jitomirskaya–Zworski) relied on reducing to scalar quasi-periodic Jacobi operators; the kagome lattice, a line graph of the honeycomb with triangles that pick up flux, does not obviously reduce this way and has a flat band at zero field. A proof would test how far the Ten Martini machinery reaches beyond scalar-reducible lattices, and the kagome butterfly is studied in cold-atom and materials physics.
issues: Original M left the flux distribution unspecified; for a uniform field the triangle flux is 1/8 of the cell flux, so the spectrum is 8-periodic (not 1-periodic) in alpha, and line-graph reductions to honeycomb only work when triangle flux is trivial. Made the Peierls phases explicit. Quick numerics (rational alpha up to 2/5, 3L^2-site tori) show the zero-field flat band at E=-2 disappears for nonzero flux, so there is no isolated infinitely degenerate eigenvalue spoiling perfection; spectrum shows 3q subbands. Literature: Helffer–Kerdelhué–Royo-Letelier treat Hou's kagome model (Chambers formula, band non-overlap) but no Cantor spectrum result found for kagome.

title: Blank jigsaw with few edge shapes
W: A jigsaw with no picture can only be solved from the shapes of its pieces. Each internal edge is one of k shapes (a tab that fits only its own matching blank), and pieces may be turned. How small can k be if some n×n blank jigsaw still goes together in exactly one way? Counting shows k must be at least about √n, and random puzzles need about n.
M: An $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types is a map assigning to each internal edge of the $n\times n$ grid a type in $[k]$ and an orientation (which side carries the tab); border edges are flat. Its pieces are the $n^2$ unit squares, each regarded as a distinct physical object carrying its four (type, tab/blank) labels up to rotation. An assembly is a placement of all pieces bijectively on the cells, each rotated by a multiple of $90^\circ$, so that every internal edge joins a tab and a blank of the same type and all flat edges lie on the border. Let $k(n)$ be the least $k$ for which some $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types has exactly one assembly up to the four rotations of the whole square. Determine the order of $k(n)$; in particular, is $k(n)=\Theta(\sqrt n)$?
why: Uniqueness of jigsaw reconstruction is a well-studied model problem for shotgun assembly (Mossel–Ross; Bordenave–Feige–Mossel; Nenadov–Pfister–Steger), but all known thresholds concern random puzzles, where about n edge types are needed. Since unique assembly forces all n^2 pieces to be distinct, a simple count gives k(n) ≥ c√n, so the question is whether designed puzzles can beat random ones by a polynomial factor, a rigidity/design question in the spirit of de Bruijn tori.
issues: Original M was ambiguous: whether identical pieces count as interchangeable (unlabelled multiset, where swapping identical pieces is not a new assembly) changes the answer completely; fixed to distinct physical pieces, which forces all pieces distinct and gives the counting lower bound k(n) ≥ c n^{1/2}. Random-puzzle results give k(n) ≤ (1+o(1))n. Found no deterministic-design result. The unlabelled variant (constant k possible?) is a separate, also interesting question, related to tile-complexity results in self-assembly. Risk: an explicit coordinate-encoding construction may give Θ(√n) fairly routinely.

title: An explicit, checkable counterexample to Hadwiger's conjecture
W: Hadwiger's conjecture says a graph that needs t colours contains the complete graph K_t as a minor. A disproof claimed in October 2026 (not yet peer reviewed) is non-constructive: it uses graphs with no three pairwise non-adjacent vertices, on roughly 2^(10^12) vertices or more, and never names a graph. Find one concrete graph on fewer than a million vertices for which the conjecture fails, with a proof that can be checked.
M: For a finite graph $G$ let $h(G)=\max\{t: K_t\preceq G\}$ be its Hadwiger number and $\chi(G)$ its chromatic number. Exhibit an explicit graph $G$ with $|V(G)|<10^6$ and $h(G)<\chi(G)$, together with a verifiable certificate of both bounds. (Equivalently decide: is $\min\{|V(G)|: h(G)<\chi(G)\}<10^6$? A natural candidate class is $\alpha(G)\le 2$, where $\chi(G)\ge |V(G)|/2$ and it suffices to show $h(G)<|V(G)|/2$.)
why: Hadwiger's conjecture (1943) is one of the central problems of graph theory, generalizing the Four Colour Theorem; a disproof would reshape the theory of minors and colouring. A non-constructive counterexample of tower-like size tells us little about where the conjecture fails, while an explicit moderate-size one would be checkable, would independently confirm the claim, and would show which structures (e.g. dense graphs with independence number 2, Seymour's test case) actually break it.
issues: Premise checked: the only claimed disproof found is in OpenAI's October 2026 bulk release (Family 157 in the survey arXiv 2610.17090): non-constructive, alpha(G)≤2, m = 2^(1000·g·M0·n) with g = 10^9+1, h(G) < 26m/75 + 2/3; not peer reviewed. The odd, list and dominating Hadwiger variants have separate disproofs, which do not refute the original. The original 'or prove every counterexample is larger' half is hopeless (it would prove HC for all graphs under 10^6 vertices, including χ up to ~10^6) and the 10^6 cutoff is arbitrary, so reframed as an explicit, certified construction. Caveat: if the claimed disproof is wrong, the problem becomes essentially Hadwiger's conjecture itself. Certifying h(G) < χ(G) for a large dense graph is itself nontrivial (Hadwiger number is NP-hard), so the certificate is part of the task. Known: HC holds for t ≤ 6 (Robertson–Seymour–Thomas), so χ(G) ≥ 7 is necessary.

title: Is the Mandelbrot set decidable at Gaussian rationals?
W: Is there an algorithm that takes a complex number with rational real and imaginary parts and decides whether it lies in the Mandelbrot set? Escaping points can be confirmed, and so can points that have an attracting or neutral cycle of some period, since for each period that is an exact algebraic check. The trouble is points on the boundary where every cycle repels. No such Gaussian rational is known, but none has been ruled out.
M: Let $M=\{c\in\mathbb C:(f_c^{n}(0))_{n\ge0}\text{ bounded}\}$, $f_c(z)=z^2+c$. Prove or disprove that $M\cap\mathbb Q(i)$ is a decidable subset of $\mathbb Q(i)$ (with the standard encoding of Gaussian rationals). Since $\mathbb Q(i)\setminus M$ is recursively enumerable, and for each $n$ the existence of an $n$-cycle of $f_c$ with multiplier of modulus $\le1$ is decidable for algebraic $c$ (Tarski), a positive answer would follow from: (*) every $c\in M\cap\mathbb Q(i)$ has a non-repelling cycle. Prove or disprove (*). (Example: $c=\mu/2-\mu^2/4=(37+16i)/100$ with $\mu=(3+4i)/5$ has a fixed point of multiplier $\mu$, not a root of unity, so $c\in\partial M$. Centres and Misiurewicz parameters are algebraic integers, so the only ones in $\mathbb Q(i)$ lie in $\mathbb Z[i]$.)
why: M is not decidable in the Blum–Shub–Smale model, and its computability as a set (Hertling) is tied to the density-of-hyperbolicity conjecture. Restricting to exact rational inputs gives the most concrete version of 'can a computer decide the Mandelbrot set?', and leads to an arithmetic-dynamics question: can a non-escaping Gaussian rational have only repelling cycles (be non-hyperbolic, e.g. infinitely renormalizable or Collet–Eckmann-like)?
issues: Not novel: Potgieter, 'Hypercomputing the Mandelbrot set?' (arXiv cs/0604003, Sect. 2.3 'A rational refuge?') asks exactly whether M ∩ Q^2 is decidable, leaves it open and guesses no. Found no later resolution. Added the reduction to (*) (escape semi-decidable; non-repelling cycle of given period decidable for algebraic c), which shows the real difficulty. Verified the example computation. Real rationals are trivial (M ∩ R = [-2, 1/4]), so only non-real Gaussian rationals matter. The multiplier (3+4i)/5 = e^{2πiθ} has θ Diophantine by Baker's theorem, so that example is a Siegel parameter.

title: A strongly aperiodic monotile in four dimensions
W: The hat (2023) is a single shape that tiles the plane only non-periodically, and in 2026 a 3D analogue was announced (Chair44, a decorated chair-shaped polycube). Find one connected 4D shape whose copies fill 4D space, where no tiling by it is left unchanged by any translation.
M: Find a compact set $T\subset\mathbb R^4$ that is the closure of its interior and homeomorphic to a closed 4-ball (or at least connected), such that (i) $\mathbb R^4$ admits a tiling by isometric copies of $T$ (reflections allowed), and (ii) no tiling of $\mathbb R^4$ by isometric copies of $T$ is invariant under any nonzero translation (strong aperiodicity). (Weaker variant: (ii') no tiling is invariant under a rank-4 lattice of translations.)
why: Aperiodic monotiles are now known in dimension 2 (Smith–Myers–Kaplan–Goodman-Strauss) and claimed in dimension 3 (Tsiokos's Chair44, 2026, in the strong sense), and Greenfeld–Tao give translational tiles that cannot tile periodically in very high dimension. Whether a single connected tile can force aperiodicity in every dimension, and in particular in R^4, is the next natural step. Kamenetsky's 2026 computer search for 4D chair markings came up empty, which suggests the 3D method does not simply extend.
issues: Original M ('admits no periodic tiling') was ambiguous between weak and strong aperiodicity. The weak form may be close to routine: the prism Chair44 × [0,1] tiles R^4 with a period only in the last direction, so one only has to rule out non-layered tilings by it. Strengthened to strong aperiodicity, which a prism cannot achieve. Literature: 3D strong monotile claimed (arXiv 2609.19214; matching rules arXiv 2609.23783; notes 2609.24779). Kamenetsky (arXiv 2610.00916, AI-assisted) poses a 4D marked-chair problem (Problem 9.1) and conjectures unmarked polyhedral prototiles for every N ≥ 4 (Conj. 9.2), so the problem has been posed but is open, and not novel.

title: Simple closed geodesics on the Fermat quartic surface
W: On the surface x⁴+y⁴+z⁴ = 1 the nine symmetry planes cut out nine simple closed geodesics, and there are at least four more: non-planar hexagonal ones that wind around the four body diagonals. Does the surface have only finitely many simple closed geodesics?
M: Let $S=\{x^4+y^4+z^4=1\}\subset\mathbb R^3$ with the induced metric (convex, Gaussian curvature $K\ge0$ with $K=0$ exactly on $S\cap\{xyz=0\}$). Besides the nine planar geodesics cut by $x=0,y=0,z=0,x=\pm y,y=\pm z,x=\pm z$, $S$ carries four non-planar simple closed geodesics, the orbit under the octahedral group of a geodesic invariant under the permutations of coordinates and $-I$. Decide whether $S$ has finitely many simple closed geodesics (as unparametrized curves), and if so determine their number.
why: Lusternik–Schnirelmann guarantees three simple closed geodesics on any convex sphere, and the round sphere has infinitely many, but deciding the full count for an explicit non-round convex surface is rarely possible. This surface has large symmetry and curvature vanishing along three curves, so it is a concrete test case for counting and symmetry methods, but the specific choice is somewhat arbitrary.
issues: The original second part ('whether these nine are all') is false. Shooting numerically (RK, tol 1e-12) from {x=y}∩S orthogonally to that plane until hitting {y=z} orthogonally gives an arc from (0.38,0.38,-0.84)/norm to (0.980,-0.443,-0.443). Reflecting it closes up (closure error 7e-9) to a simple, non-planar closed geodesic of length about 7.43 that winds around the (1,1,1) axis, is invariant under S3 and -I, and has an orbit of size 4. So there are at least 13. Also K=0 along the coordinate-plane curves (K ∝ x²y²z²), worth noting. No literature found on this surface. Statement corrected; the finiteness question remains but is niche and probably hard without being illuminating.

title: Lonely runner gap for the first n primes
W: With the first n primes as speeds, find the loneliness gap asymptotically. (Trivial: the gap equals 1/4 for every n ≥ 4.)
M: $\delta_n=\sup_{t\in\mathbb R}\min_{i\le n}\|tp_i\|$, where $p_i$ is the $i$-th prime. Answer: $\delta_1=\tfrac12,\ \delta_2=\tfrac25,\ \delta_3=\tfrac27$, and $\delta_n=\tfrac14$ for all $n\ge4$.
why: None. The arithmetic of the primes mod 4 settles it at once.
issues: Trivial. At t=1/4 we get ||2t|| = 1/2 and ||pt|| = 1/4 for every odd p, so δ_n ≥ 1/4 for all n. δ_n is non-increasing in n, and an exact computation (candidate maximizers t = m/(p_i+p_j) and (2k+1)/(2p_i)) gives δ_4 = 1/4 for speeds {2,3,5,7}. Hence δ_n = 1/4 for n ≥ 4 (checked numerically up to n=80). Without the prime 2 it is even more trivial: t=1/2 gives δ=1/2 for any set of odd speeds. The real lonely-runner content is in lower bounds over all speed sets (Tao's 1/(2n)+c log n/(n^2 (log log n)^2)), not in this case.

title: A Jörgens theorem for the Hessian permanent
W: Jörgens proved that a convex function on the whole plane whose Hessian determinant is 1 must be a quadratic polynomial. Replace the determinant by the permanent, u_xx·u_yy + u_xy², and ask whether the same rigidity holds for solutions on the elliptic branch.
M: Let $u\in C^4(\mathbb R^2)$ satisfy $u_{xx}u_{yy}+u_{xy}^2=1$, $u_{xx}>0$ and $2u_{xy}^2<1$ on $\mathbb R^2$ (these are exactly the conditions for the linearized operator $u_{yy}\partial_{xx}+2u_{xy}\partial_{xy}+u_{xx}\partial_{yy}$ to be elliptic; they force $u$ convex with $0<\det D^2u=1-2u_{xy}^2\le1$). Prove or disprove that $u$ is a quadratic polynomial.
why: Jörgens' theorem and its extensions (Calabi, Pogorelov; Yuan's work on special Lagrangian equations) depend on the Monge–Ampère or Lagrangian structure, which allows Lewy or Legendre-type transformations to linear or holomorphic problems. The permanent level set {ac+b²=1} is a one-sheeted hyperboloid. It is not a symplectic Monge–Ampère equation, its ellipticity degenerates both at infinity and at the finite boundary 2b²=1, and in two dimensions Liouville theorems are known in general only for uniformly elliptic F (Nirenberg). So this is a clean test of whether 2D Bernstein–Jörgens rigidity needs the special structure.
issues: Checked ellipticity: the symbol [[u_yy,u_xy],[u_xy,u_xx]] is positive definite iff u_xx>0 and u_xx u_yy - u_xy² = 1 - 2u_xy² > 0, so the stated conditions are right and imply convexity. Ruled out simple non-quadratic candidates: separable u=f(x)+g(y)+bxy; u=φ(x)+yψ(x)+y²χ(x) (forces χ ∝ x^{1/3}, not entire); quadratic plus a plane wave f(αx+βy) (forces u_xy² = 1, not elliptic). The equation is not of symplectic Monge–Ampère type (not linear in the Plücker coordinates (1,a,b,c,ac-b²)), so no Sp(4) reduction to Jörgens. The partial Legendre transform gives 2v_py² - v_pp v_yy = v_pp², not linear. Found no literature on this equation; known 2D Liouville theorems (Li–Liang, Nirenberg) need uniform ellipticity, which fails here.

title: Infinitely many knot types in the symmetric ABC flow
W: Steady Euler flows can carry knotted streamlines, and generic high-frequency Beltrami fields on the torus contain every knot. Show that the most-studied explicit example, the ABC flow with A = B = C = 1, has closed streamlines tied in infinitely many different knots.
M: Let $X=(\sin z+\cos y,\ \sin x+\cos z,\ \sin y+\cos x)$ on $\mathbb T^3=(\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z)^3$ (a curl eigenfield, $\nabla\times X=X$). Prove that the periodic orbits of $X$ that lie in some embedded 3-ball $B\subset\mathbb T^3$ realize infinitely many distinct knot types (as knots in $B\cong$ a ball in $\mathbb R^3$). Stronger: every knot type is realized.
why: The ABC flow with A=B=C=1 is the standard model of Lagrangian chaos in steady Euler flows and of fast-dynamo theory, yet rigorous results on its dynamics are mostly perturbative (near integrable parameters) or about non-contractible orbits. Etnyre–Ghrist and Enciso–Peralta-Salas proved that some steady Euler or Beltrami flows realize all knots, using perturbations or random high-frequency fields. Proving it for this explicit lowest-frequency field would most likely need a computer-assisted horseshoe plus template theory (Birman–Williams), turning numerical evidence of chaos into topological information.
issues: Clarified knot type for orbits in T^3 by requiring them to lie in an embedded ball (null-homotopy alone does not give a well-defined classical knot type). Literature: Etnyre–Ghrist (math-ph/9906021) start from the ABC field with A=1, B=1/2, C=0 perturbed, and transplant a horseshoe to a metric on S^3, not the symmetric ABC on T^3. Dombre et al. and arXiv 1601.02724 give periodic orbits with rotation vectors along the axes (non-contractible). Szumiński–Llibre (2609.17449) is perturbative near the axes. Enciso–Peralta-Salas–Romaniega (2006.15033) handle random high-frequency Beltrami fields. Found no result on knotted contractible orbits of the A=B=C=1 flow. Likely approachable by rigorous numerics, so more a hard technical target than a conceptual breakthrough.
